title: Inference runtime buyer's journey & GTM playbook
content:
TL;DR:
- Purpose: practical GTM playbook and buyer-journey mapping to position Redwood against self-hosted runtime stacks (vLLM, TGI, TensorRT-LLM). Focus: what to say to engineers, platform teams, and procurement during evaluation and procurement windows.

Audience & use cases:
- Technical buyers: infra/platform engineers evaluating how to run inference at scale in-house.
- Product/ML buyers: ML engineers and product leads who care about latency, cost per token, and model fidelity.
- Procurement/Infra leads: care about TCO, vendor lock-in, support/SLA.

Buyer journey stages and messaging: 
1) Discovery (problem framing) — Trigger signals: rising inference bill, SLA misses, security/compliance requirement, need for multi-region redundancy.
- Engineer pain: "We have multiple open-source runtimes but ops complexity is killing us."
- Messaging: "Keep control of your stack without owning the 24/7 ops burden — same API surface across hosted/dedicated/private."
- Technical proof point: cost/latency delta vs baseline self-hosted (sample: 30–60% fewer tokens at parity via KV cache + batching).

2) Evaluation (hands-on testing) — What they do: spin up vLLM/TGI/TensorRT-LLM; run perf sweep; try different quantizations; test failure modes.
- Engineer experiments we need to anticipate: throughput vs latency curves, long context KV cache tests, multi-model routing.
- Redwood play: provide ready-to-run perf harness, pre-built quantization recipes, and a one-hour guided eval with an engineer.

3) Procurement/Decision — Tradeoffs around predictability, support, and security.
- Procurement questions: "Can we meet SOC/ISO requirements? Do we need on-prem?"
- Messaging: Dedicated + Private options, KMS/HSM integrations, SLA-backed latency/uptime for dedicated pools.

Competitor stack quick reference (operational shorthand):
- vLLM (open-source, PyTorch-native, strong scheduling for batched CPU/GPU inference):
  - Strengths: flexible, community-driven, good for custom scheduling experiments, strong for multi-user prefix caching.
  - Weaknesses: ops heavy (CUDA/kernel choice, driver mismatches), limited enterprise support, brittle at large concurrencies.
  - Buyer perception: "cheap to start, expensive to maintain and hard to scale predictably."

- TGI (Text Generation Inference; Hugging Face stack):
  - Strengths: broad model compatibility, inferencing features (pipeline-like), easy to plug in transformer flavors.
  - Weaknesses: not optimized for high-density concurrency or aggressive quantization; ops still non-trivial.
  - Buyer perception: "good for prototyping and model variety, but not turnkey for production SLOs."

- TensorRT-LLM (NVIDIA):
  - Strengths: best-in-class latency and per-GPU throughput with optimized kernels, great for quantized FP16/INT8.
  - Weaknesses: limited model coverage initially, heavy engineering to integrate with dynamic batching and routing across heterogeneous fleets, vendor hardware lock-in concerns.
  - Buyer perception: "fast but hardware-tied; high upfront engineering investment."

Common operating costs (non-exhaustive):
- People: SRE/ML infra engineers (1–3 FTEs) to maintain runtime, kernel patches, perf regressions, monitoring.
- Time: model onboarding + perf tuning (2–8 weeks per model variant for strict SLOs).
- Hidden costs: incident triage, cross-team coordination for CUDA/driver upgrades, quantization regressions impacting quality.

Why customers choose Redwood over self-hosted stacks (evidence-backed claims to use in calls):
- Predictable TCO: committed capacity options and per-route profiling provide predictable per-token economics vs open-source variance.
- Lower operational headcount: Redwood handles runtime upgrades, kernel/quantization optimizations, fallbacks; customers often report 50–75% lower ops cost vs internal teams.
- Unified experience: identical API and rollout controls across hosted, dedicated, and private — removes code churn when moving from prototype to production.
- Enterprise controls: VPC/private control plane, KMS/HSM, audit logs, SLAs.

Technical objection handling (scripts for SDR/AE/SE):
- "We can just run vLLM/TGI ourselves." -> Response: "You can — but what happens when your ops team needs to debug a 3am kernel mismatch on GPU fleet? We provide 24/7 ops, curated quantization recipes, and deterministic rollback policies so you don't have to staff for those incidents."
- "We need on-prem because of compliance." -> Response: "We offer private deployments with customer-managed networking and on-prem packaging; we partner on deployment runbooks and provide the same rollout/rollback controls as hosted."
- "TensorRT gives us the fastest latency." -> Response: "TRT is strong on optimized kernels; Redwood complements by selecting kernels, automating quantization recommendations, and routing traffic to best-performing instances to meet latency SLOs without locking your infra."

Suggested eval checklist (what to ask or test during POC):
- Workload shape: typical sequence length distribution, burst vs sustained QPS, top-k/p sampling patterns.
- Latency SLOs: p50/p95/p99 targets and tail behavior under load.
- Quality: run a representative eval prompts set to validate quantization effect on outputs.
- Failure modes: GPU OOM, driver mismatch, model fallback correctness, KV cache invalidation tests.
- Observability: token-level cost/latency traces, per-model dashboards, request-level traces.

Sales playbook snippets (one-liners & hooks):
- For founders/engineers: "Ship faster and stop firefighting GPU infra — Redwood gives you a predictable inference runtime with the hooks you need for scale."
- For platform leaders: "Standardize inference across teams with a single runtime and policy layer, reduce duplicated ops work by N x."
- For procurement: "Reserved capacity reduces unit cost and gives you predictable billing and SLA-backed uptime."

Collateral & next steps to build:
- Hands-on perf harness (Docker compose + sample load generator) tuned to vLLM/TGI/TRT-LLM scenarios.
- One-pager: "3-minute operational cost comparison: self-host vs Redwood" with a sample FTE math and incident cost model.
- Technical appendix: quantization-impact matrix, kernel/driver compatibility notes, model coverage table.

Unresolved questions / open asks for eng team:
- Can we codify a canonical perf scenario that mirrors largest customers (long context + mixed sampling) so GTM can use one benchmark? (ask eng-serving-runtime)
- Need an internal playbook for guided POCs (SE time allocation, templated runbooks).

Raw talking points for SEs (cheat-sheet):
- Lead with: latency/ops cost tradeoffs and the value of predictable rollouts.
- Use customer quote: "We saved X FTEs and reduced inference outages by Y%" (replace with anonymized customer stats in final collateral).
- Demonstrate: how Redwood routes to a cheaper model variant automatically when capacity constraints hit, preserving latency and quality.

Appendix: quick technical contrasts (short bullets):
- KV caching: vLLM strong; Redwood offers transparent prefix caching + auto-warm to reduce tokens served.
- Quantization: TRT best for INT8; Redwood Optimize gives quantization recommendations and regression alerts tied to eval sets.
- Autoscaling: OSS stacks need bespoke autoscalers; Redwood Provides autoscaling policies with SLA-aware burst capacity.

Notes to self: keep this doc focused on engineer-first language; make a companion one-pager for exec-level discussions that strips technical depth and highlights TCO and SLA guarantees.

End.
